strengths: NCI offers a useful, simple post-hoc detector: classifier-weight alignment and a feature-norm term require only O(P) additional scoring work, without a nearest-neighbor feature bank. Table 1b reports latency close to MSP, supporting its practical appeal.

The evaluation covers CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with ResNet, DenseNet, ViT, and Swin models, including near- and far-OOD datasets. This is substantial experimental breadth. The code link and supplementary implementation descriptions also support reproducibility.

The ResNet results demonstrate a favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoff: Table 1b reports average AUROC of 89.51 versus 88.16 for ViM and 88.15 for Scale. Table 9 also reports strong DenseNet results. These contributions have value without winning every individual benchmark.

The ablations support the complementary value of the score components. In Table 6, adding the norm term improves ImageNet AUROC from 84.41 to 88.56, exceeding standalone L1 scoring at 78.91 and KNN plus L1 at 86.37. Table 7 also supports the proposed proximity score over the tested alternatives.
weaknesses: The central explanation for feature norms is mathematically unsupported. Sections 3.1–3.2 claim that forming an ETF requires features to lie sufficiently far from the origin, but ETF geometry is preserved under arbitrary positive scaling. Neural collapse also imposes no constraint on unseen OOD features. Furthermore, the ETF argument concerns centered class means, whereas the detector uses the uncentered norm ||h||1. The experiments support this term as a useful heuristic, but do not establish the claimed explanation.

Theorem 3.1 states stronger convergence than its proof establishes. Equation (4) establishes normalized alignment; obtaining the unnormalized convergence in Equation (2) requires additional control of class-mean norms or convergence rates. This does not invalidate the angular score, but weakens the formal contribution. The extension from training-feature collapse to ID/OOD separation remains empirical, and Appendix 13 reproduces prior work's plots rather than measuring collapse on the evaluated checkpoints.

Several numerical summaries are internally inconsistent. In Table 2, NCI's five ViT AUROCs average to 94.84, rather than the reported 93.64; KNN's five Swin AUROCs average to 72.58, rather than 75.88. Table 9 reports an Energy CIFAR-100 FPR95 average of 94.47 although its entries average to 64.47. These discrepancies do not establish that NCI performs poorly, but leave uncertainty about the underlying results and central aggregate-performance claims.

The conceptual advance is relatively modest: Equation (6) reduces to a centered predicted-class logit divided by the centered feature norm, while self-duality and norm-based OOD cues have cited precedents. The manuscript does not isolate its claimed benefit from centering through an uncentered ablation. NECO, the closest neural-collapse baseline, is also absent from the transformer comparisons.

Narrower reporting issues affect reproducibility: ImageNet KNN latency is copied from another paper without establishing matched timing conditions, and Appendix 9's ViM formula omits the energy term described in the text. These are distinct from the main scientific concerns. Overall, the useful detector and substantial empirical evidence place the work near acceptance, but the unsupported geometric explanation and unresolved quantitative inconsistencies keep my recommendation borderline.
